model.label: Government-run social health insurance in two main schemes (compulsory for employees, voluntary and subsidised for other residents), with medical assistance for the poor

overview.statement: China began its current round of health reform in 2009 with the aim of giving everyone basic health care coverage by the end of 2020.

Public coverage was built on three basic schemes: NRCMS (the New Rural Cooperative Medical Scheme), URBMI (Urban Resident Basic Medical Insurance) and Urban Employee Basic Medical Insurance. In 2016 the government merged NRCMS and URBMI into one urban and rural residents' scheme, and in 2018 it created the National Healthcare Security Administration to manage the schemes in a unified way.

locator.section: Main reform initiatives: health insurance system

overview.statement: With the 2009 reform, China committed to equal access to basic health care of reasonable quality with financial protection for all citizens, and the government has since increased its health funding fourfold.

According to a 2025 study, the urban-rural residents' scheme enrols nearly 960 million people, about 80% of them rural residents, while around 5% of the population (nearly 50 million people) remains uninsured.

The residents' scheme is open to every urban and rural resident not covered by employee insurance. Employee insurance is compulsory by law and funded partly by employers, while joining the residents' scheme is voluntary.
At the end of 2024, 1,326.6 million people were enrolled in basic medical insurance, and the enrolment rate was held at 95%.
At the end of 2024 the employee scheme had 379.5 million members, 8.5 million more than a year earlier: 274.9 million in work and 104.6 million retired.
The urban and rural residents' scheme had 947.1 million members at the end of 2024.

locator.section: 1(2) Urban and rural residents' basic medical insurance: enrolment

overview.statement: Article 5 of the Basic Medical and Health Care and Health Promotion Law gives citizens a legal right to receive basic medical and health services from the state and society, and commits the state to building a basic health care system that protects this right.

Under the same law, basic medical services are paid for mainly by the basic medical insurance fund and by individuals; citizens have both a right and a duty to join basic medical insurance, with employers and employees paying contributions to the employee scheme and urban and rural residents paying contributions to the residents' scheme.

The law sets out a multi-tier system: basic medical insurance is the main pillar, supplemented by others including commercial health insurance, medical assistance, employee mutual-aid schemes and medical charity, with medical assistance meant to secure basic care for eligible people in hardship.

The Social Insurance Law requires employees to join employee medical insurance, with contributions shared by employer and employee; self-employed people without staff, part-time workers not enrolled through an employer, and other people in flexible work may join and pay the contribution themselves.

financing.statement: The minimum yearly individual contribution to residents' insurance has risen from 10 yuan per person when it was introduced in 2003 to 380 yuan by 2024, while rural residents' disposable income averaged 23,119 yuan in 2024; the authors find the rising contributions a significant burden for rural families.

As described in the 2015 WHO/Asia Pacific Observatory review, all urban employers and their employees, including retirees, must join the employee scheme, with contributions of at least 2% of salary from the employee and 6% from the employer.

locator.section: 3.3 Sources of revenue: social insurance contribution

financing.statement: The 2015 review notes that each local government, usually at the prefecture-level city, sets the actual employee-scheme contribution rate, and that retirees pay no contribution.

locator.section: 3.3 Sources of revenue: social insurance contribution

financing.statement: The 2015 review reported that the two residents' schemes of that time, URBMI and NRCMS, were funded by premiums and by government, with government subsidies playing the dominant role.

In 2024 the basic medical insurance funds (including maternity insurance) took in 3,491.3 billion yuan and spent 2,976.4 billion yuan; the pooled funds ran a surplus of 463.9 billion yuan for the year and held 3,862.9 billion yuan in accumulated reserves.

locator.section: 1. Basic medical insurance (fund revenue and spending)

financing.statement: The residents' scheme's fund took in 1,118.1 billion yuan in 2024 and spent 1,066.1 billion yuan, leaving a surplus of 51.9 billion yuan for the year and 818.3 billion yuan accumulated.

locator.section: 1(2) Urban and rural residents' basic medical insurance: fund revenue and spending

financing.statement: Total health expenditure in 2025 is preliminarily estimated at 9,336.7 billion yuan (6,637.9 yuan per person, 6.7% of GDP): 25.2% from government health spending, 47.7% from 'social' health spending and 27.1% paid by individuals.

covered.statement: By 2018, over 95% of China's population was enrolled in a social health insurance scheme.
The national insurance drug list had grown to 2,643 medicines by 2019, and per-person government subsidies for the residents' schemes in 2018 were more than five times their 2009 level.
A government-funded basic public health package is offered to nearly everyone; it grew from 9 service categories in 2009 to 14 in 2017, and funding rose from ¥15 per person in 2009 to ¥55 in 2018.

Under national procurement, the manufacturers that win a tender are guaranteed 60-70% of the previous year's total use of that drug, which gives the public payer strong bargaining power over manufacturers.

Decisions on which drugs are reimbursed have become more centralised: provincial routes were removed, the National Healthcare Security Administration was created, and the National Reimbursement Drug List is now the main way a drug gets covered.

Since national price negotiations began in 2017, the average price reductions achieved in the annual negotiations for the reimbursement list have ranged from 44% to 61%; in 2020, 704 drugs passed initial review, 162 were shortlisted and 119 were successfully negotiated, a 17% success rate.

locator.section: HTA decision making, reimbursement and price negotiation

covered.statement: According to the authors, listing decisions weigh a drug's innovation, added clinical benefit and cost-effectiveness compared with standard care, the level of unmet need, and the budget impact on the basic insurance funds, in some respects like many other national health technology assessment systems.
The social insurance schemes built from 1998 onwards for urban employees and for urban and rural residents differed in scope and mainly covered inpatient care.

By law, the national healthcare security authority sets what the basic insurance fund pays for, after hearing the health, traditional Chinese medicine, drug regulation and finance authorities, among others; provinces may add specific items and standards within national rules and must file them; and the authority must run evidence-based clinical and economic evaluations of listed drugs, procedures and service facility standards, whose results are the basis for changing coverage.

The 2024 national reimbursement drug list contained 3,159 medicines (1,765 Western medicines and 1,394 Chinese patent medicines), 91 of them added in 2024; over seven yearly revisions since the National Healthcare Security Administration was set up in 2018, 835 medicines have been added.
By the end of 2024, 31 provinces and the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps had brought assisted reproduction into medical insurance coverage.

The Social Insurance Law excludes from basic medical insurance any costs that the work-injury fund, a liable third party or public health funding should bear, and care received outside China; where a liable third party does not pay or cannot be identified, the fund pays first and may then recover the cost.

cost_sharing.statement: Two supplementary layers sit on top of basic insurance: Medical Financial Assistance for people in poverty, started in 2003, and Catastrophic Medical Insurance for patients with catastrophic illness, started in 2012.

locator.section: Main reform initiatives: health insurance system

cost_sharing.statement: Insurance reimbursement for a procured drug is set by the winning bid's price: patients who take the winning manufacturer's product pay a small share, while those who choose another version pay the difference in price themselves.

According to the 2015 review, the basic schemes reimburse eligible hospital costs and outpatient costs for severe diseases subject to deductibles, co-payments and ceilings; insured people pay out of pocket for items outside the reimbursement list, deductibles, co-payments and costs above the ceiling.

Local governments have wide latitude in designing outpatient pooling, so its timing, deductibles, reimbursement rates and caps vary by place: under the employee scheme, Beijing and Shanghai began outpatient co-payment policies as early as 2001, while some cities had not started such policies by 2018.
In 2024 the employee scheme paid 84.8% of members' inpatient costs that fall within the reimbursement lists (83.8% in tertiary, 87.6% in secondary and 89.9% in primary or lower-level facilities).

In 2024 the residents' scheme paid 68.6% of members' in-list inpatient costs: 64.1% in tertiary hospitals, 73.3% in secondary and 81.5% in primary or lower-level facilities. These rates cover only costs within the lists, not total spending.

locator.section: 1(2) Urban and rural residents' basic medical insurance: benefits

financial_hardship.statement: In 2018, medical assistance funds spent ¥42.46 billion nationally: they paid insurance contributions for 76.7 million people and helped 53.6 million people with outpatient and inpatient costs.
A 2023 Lancet Public Health assessment found that catastrophic health spending is unusually common in China compared with countries at a similar level of economic development.

A study of 28 provinces using the 2017 China Household Finance Survey estimated that 11.0% of households nationally had catastrophic health expenditure, ranging from 6.3% in Beijing to 16.0% in Heilongjiang, and that 2.0% experienced medical impoverishment, from 0.03% in Shanghai to 4.6% in Anhui.

In that study, a household had catastrophic health expenditure when its health spending in a year reached at least 40% of its total spending other than food; medical impoverishment means out-of-pocket health spending left a household below, or further below, the poverty line.

Using 2015 survey data and counting only money borrowed from family, friends or third parties, a study found medical debt in 2.42% of middle-income and 3.92% of low-income households; among low-income households the average debt was 2.49 times average yearly household income, and medical debt impoverished about 10% of non-poor households.

The authors note that with this narrow definition medical debt was relatively uncommon, but that where it occurred it was a lasting burden, pushing many low- and middle-income households into poverty and committing them to years of repayments.

In 2024 medical assistance spent 79.2 billion yuan: it paid basic insurance contributions for 79.2 million people (not counting subsidies paid by other departments) and gave outpatient or inpatient help 180.9 million times, averaging 1,254 yuan per inpatient episode and 92 yuan per outpatient one.

additional_care.statement: City-customised 'inclusive commercial health insurance' plans use community rating and low premiums (on average under 0.28% of disposable income per person in 2021), have no age or occupation limits and no strict exclusions for pre-existing conditions, and cover large costs left after basic insurance, up to a benefit ceiling of 1 million yuan.

These plans are underwritten by groups of large insurers under local government guidance, with government help in design, promotion and data sharing; by the end of 2021 they ran in 244 prefecture-level cities with about 140 million cumulative enrolments (renewals included), but the authors put national enrolment at only around 5%, too low for a sustainable risk pool.

Long-term care insurance began in Qingdao in 2012 and was piloted in 15 locations in phases in 2016 and 2018; by the end of 2022 the pilot cities had 16.99 million members and 12.08 million people receiving care.
In 2024, long-term care insurance in 49 pilot cities had 187.9 million members and 1.46 million people receiving benefits, with fund revenue of 24.4 billion yuan and spending of 13.1 billion yuan.

access.statement: Between 2012 and 2017, the primary care workforce grew by 7.1% to 3.863 million, and general practitioners rose from 0.8 to 1.8 per 10,000 people.

Primary care providers are usually neither patients' first point of contact nor coordinators of specialist care; primary care facilities handled 53% of outpatient visits in 2018, down from 62% in 2010.
The 2015 review found no gatekeeping: patients can go directly to any hospital, which crowds tertiary hospitals while primary care is underused.
The 2015 review described general practice as still in its infancy and severely short-staffed, with 109,794 GPs in 2012.
The number of general practitioners in mainland China grew from 109,794 in 2012 to 434,868 in 2021, or 3.08 per 10,000 people.
GPs remain unevenly spread across regions; the western region has too few relative both to its population and to its land area.
In 2025 China had 3.78 practising physicians (including assistant physicians) and 4.32 registered nurses per 1,000 people, and 4.91 general practitioners per 10,000 people.
Of the 10.65 billion visits to health facilities in 2025, tertiary hospitals handled 3.04 billion and primary-level facilities 5.65 billion.
By the end of 2025, among public hospitals at secondary level and above, 64.6% offered appointment booking, 67.5% provided telemedicine and 92.4% mutually recognised test and examination results.

The basic health law commits the state to building a tiered care system step by step: non-emergency patients are to be guided to primary care first, with responsibility for first contact and review of referrals, two-way referral between levels, and links to basic medical insurance.
In 2024 insured people made 397 million general outpatient and emergency, chronic-disease outpatient and inpatient visits outside the area where they were insured, costing 786.8 billion yuan.

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2016 Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index, China sat in the eighth of ten deciles nationally, but its provinces ranged from the top decile (Beijing, 91.5) to the fourth (Tibet, 48.0), with eastern provinces scoring higher than western ones.
Between 1990 and 2016, China was among the middle-SDI (socio-demographic index) countries with the most pronounced gains in the HAQ Index.

A composite index of management of non-communicable diseases rose only slowly, from 62.0% in 2004 to 64.3% in 2018, with prevention lagging; all the management indicators had a low probability of reaching their 2030 targets.
Rural areas consistently had fewer health resources than urban areas and scored 2.2% lower on management of non-communicable diseases in 2018.

National maternal and child health surveillance shows a rural-urban gap in 2025: under-five mortality was 3.0 per 1,000 in cities and 6.5 in rural areas, and infant mortality 2.3 and 4.4 per 1,000, respectively.
In the GBD 2019 study, China's HAQ Index score for ages 0-74 was 70.2 (95% uncertainty interval 66.2-74.1) in 2019, 35.2 points higher than in 1990; it was 78.0 for ages 0-14 and 65.3 for ages 65-74.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; columns in order: 2019 HAQ Index (95% UI) overall 0-74, young 0-14, working 15-64, post-working 65-74; then absolute change 1990-2019 overall, young, working, post-working

costs.statement: In 2017, drugs and consumables made up 48.0% of public hospitals' total revenue (medicines alone 34.7%), while income for medical staff services was 27.5% of their medical revenue.
Between 2008 and 2018, government funding for primary care institutions grew more than tenfold, reaching ¥197 billion (it had been ¥19 billion).
By the end of 2021, national volume-based procurement had saved more than 260 billion yuan (about US$36.3 billion), according to the figures the authors cite.
Government health spending rose from 24.7% of total health spending in 2008 to 30.4% in 2020, and from 4.4% to 7.8% of all government spending over the same period.

China's total health spending passed 9 trillion yuan in 2023; the authors report that medical costs have grown by more than 10% a year, well above growth in GDP and disposable income, and that residents' out-of-pocket costs have risen despite higher reimbursement rates.

Total out-of-pocket medical spending rose from 657 billion yuan in 2009 to 1,513 billion yuan in 2017, while its share of total health spending fell from 37.46% in 2009 to under 30% by 2015 and stayed there through 2017.

In 2025 the average hospital outpatient visit cost 357.7 yuan and the average inpatient stay 9,768.9 yuan, about 1% less than in 2024 in both cases; medicines made up 36.8% of the outpatient cost and 19.1% of the inpatient cost (20.4% a year earlier).

The 2019 World Bank/WHO study projected that, if reform did not go deeper, health spending would rise in real terms from 3,531 billion yuan in 2015 to 15,805 billion yuan in 2035 (2014 prices), or from 5.3% to 9.1% of GDP, with inpatient care accounting for over 60% of the growth.

what_works.statement: A 2019 Lancet review of the decade after 2009 found substantial progress in equal access to care and in financial protection, especially for people of lower socioeconomic status.

A 2023 Lancet Public Health assessment found that coverage of maternal, newborn and child health, infectious disease services and service capacity and access is now comparable to high-income countries, with smaller inequalities than before.
Seven rounds of national volume-based drug procurement between 2018 and 2022 lowered the prices of 294 drug formulations by an average of 53%.

A cohort study found that, among middle-aged and older rural adults, the merger of the urban and rural residents' insurance schemes was associated with better self-rated health and fewer depressive symptoms.

A study of 932,354 inpatient cases in DRG pilot hospitals and 608,940 in non-pilot hospitals (November 2021 to September 2022) found that pilot hospitals did more laparoscopic surgery, used fewer low-value drugs and had fewer 30-day readmissions.
The same analysis credits strong political commitment and targeted funding for good results in reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health and in infectious diseases.
Rates of catastrophic health spending and medical impoverishment fell significantly between 2010 and 2016, according to earlier research the study cites.

The 2019 World Bank/WHO study found that after two decades of building, China's facilities, even at lower levels, had modern infrastructure and equipment, and credited the government with setting building standards and an essential-equipment inventory for village clinics, township and community health centres.

locator.section: Chapter 3: structure of the delivery system

problems.statement: A 2019 Lancet review of the reform found remaining gaps in quality of care, control of non-communicable diseases, efficiency of delivery, control of health spending, and public satisfaction.

The 2023 Lancet Public Health assessment found large gaps in chronic disease services: risk-factor control has made little progress in ten years, and coverage for most chronic conditions is below that of high-income countries.

Social health insurance pays wherever patients seek care, with no referral needed, and pays more generously for hospital care than for primary care, which encourages patients to bypass primary care and makes it hard for primary care to act as a gatekeeper.

In a study in western China using trained actors posing as patients with dysentery or angina, village doctors asked 18% of recommended questions, did 15% of recommended examinations, and correctly diagnosed 26% of cases.
Systematic reviews put the average rate of antibiotic use in primary care facilities above 50%, far above the WHO-recommended level of under 30%.

A 2020 Lancet review of primary care listed its system challenges as weak practitioner training, fee-for-service payment that rewards tests and treatment over prevention, separation of clinical care from public health services, and poor continuity of care.

Financial protection varies widely between provinces: income-related inequality was generally much lower within the developed eastern provinces than within central and western ones, and the authors call for particular attention to low-income households in central and western provinces.

Citing National Healthcare Security Administration data, a 2025 study reports that enrolment in the urban and rural residents' scheme fell each year from 2019, by 0.3%, 0.8%, 0.8% and then 2.5% in 2022, when it dropped by 25.17 million people.

A 2025 study of why rural residents withdraw from medical insurance found four main reasons: heavy cost, a scheme design seen as unfair, failing enrolment campaigns, and the influence of online information on residents' perceptions.
A 2020 study found that China's insurance benefit packages differed by region and scheme and depended heavily on how much was paid in, which limited service coverage in less developed areas.

A study of China's national DRG payment system (CHS-DRG) linked it to longer waits for surgery (by 0.18 days), more outpatient visits in the three days before admission and after discharge, and higher 30-day all-cause mortality.

A 2023 Lancet Public Health analysis attributes China's weak chronic disease control and financial protection, especially for lower-income households, to a fragmented, hospital-centred delivery system, rising costs, shallow insurance benefits, and little attention to health across other policy areas.

The 2019 World Bank/WHO study described China's delivery system as centred on hospitals and driven by volume, with many profit-seeking, poorly governed public hospitals, fragmented financing, largely passive insurance purchasers, little information on quality, and a shortage of qualified primary care workers that weakens the system's ability to prevent, detect and treat common illnesses early, refer patients and act as gatekeeper.

The study noted that the documented overuse of medical technologies and of high-margin procedures has been attributed, in the literature it cites, to fee-for-service payment, the lack of effective referral or tiered copayments, price schedules that favour drugs and high-tech procedures, concentration of staff and resources in cities, and staff bonuses tied to volume and revenue.

In 2024 the medical insurance system recovered 27.5 billion yuan of insurance funds and confirmed fraud at 2,008 institutions; working with the police it handled 3,018 cases and 10,741 suspects were arrested.

reforms.statement: By 2017 every public hospital in China had stopped adding a mark-up to the medicines it sells.

By 2017, 65% of public hospitals at level two or above had begun paying by disease category under insurance, and in 2019 the government named 30 pilot cities for diagnosis-related group (DRG) payment.

From 2012 the reform's second phase turned to the delivery system: public hospital reform (ending drug-sale mark-ups, changing fee schedules, provider payment and governance) and moving away from a hospital-centred, treatment-focused model.

In 2018 the central government launched national volume-based procurement of medicines, starting with a pilot in 11 cities (the '4+7' scheme); a year later every province of mainland China had joined.

A 2021 State Council guideline on outpatient mutual-aid under the employee scheme began nationwide rollout of pooled outpatient funds, intended to give more financial support for outpatient care and lower what individuals pay.

In 2019 China launched a nationwide program of diagnosis-related group (DRG) bundled payment covering the whole disease spectrum; the National Healthcare Security Administration officially announced it in 2020 as the CHS-DRG system.

A 2024 State Council guideline introduced waiting periods from 2025 for the residents' scheme: people who join outside the scheme's set enrolment period, or after a gap, wait a fixed 3 months before benefits start (newborns and some other groups excepted), plus generally 1 month per extra year of lapse, which can be reduced by paying missed years; after 4 or more years' lapse, even after paying missed years, the total wait is generally at least 6 months. Provinces set the details.

The same guideline rewards continuous enrolment in the residents' scheme through critical illness insurance: from 2025 the benefit cap may be lowered for members who rejoin after a gap and raised for each further continuous year once a member has 4 continuous years; members with no fund reimbursement in a year may get a higher cap the next year; each rise is generally at least 1,000 yuan, and the total rise generally may not exceed 20% of the local original cap.

locator.section: 2(3) Improving benefit policy (critical illness insurance incentives)

reforms.statement: The guideline also loosens household-registration (hukou) limits on enrolling where people live or work; super-large cities must remove hukou limits on flexible workers, migrant workers and people in new forms of employment joining basic medical insurance where they work, and must enrol them in the employee scheme there.

By the end of 2024, payment by disease group covered essentially all pooling areas and eligible providers; it applied to more than 90% of hospital discharges and about 80% of eligible inpatient insurance spending.

National volume-based procurement reached its tenth round of drugs (62 drugs) and fifth round of high-value medical consumables in 2024; by the time of the 2024 bulletin it had covered 435 drugs and 7 major categories of high-value consumables in total.

locator.section: 4(3) Centralised procurement of drugs and consumables

us_lessons.statement: Writing about other low- and middle-income countries rather than the US, the authors argue that parts of China's pooled procurement can transfer (procurement targeted by market size and drug importance, several winning suppliers, and quality checks on generics), but that it depends on a strong public drug plan with large purchasing power.

A 2025 editorial on a study of Chinese telehealth data from 2016-2020 notes that patients in less developed regions used telehealth apps to reach doctors in more developed areas such as Beijing, Shanghai and Guangdong, home to 51 of the top 100 hospitals.

The editorial argues that copying this in the US runs into state medical licensure laws, which generally allow doctors to practise only in the state that licensed them, whereas regulation of telehealth may be less strict in China.

locator.section: Expanding cardiovascular care through telemedicine (US implications)

us_lessons.statement: It concludes that the US should consider policies that expand interstate physician licensure agreements so that virtual care can reach medically underserved areas.

locator.section: Considering health equity in rural America

us_lessons.statement: The authors caution that telemedicine does not fix the underlying causes of rural health gaps, such as lower insurance coverage, low patient volumes that raise costs, and higher poverty.

locator.section: Considering health equity in rural America

us_lessons.statement: Drawing lessons for other countries from China and Vietnam, the study concludes that political commitment, sustainable funding and administrative capacity drive coverage expansion through insurance reform, and that schemes should cover essential services for every member and subsidise vulnerable groups.
